about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

params.description: time for airless soil at 1 AU to come within 1/e of full maturity, with the wind and micrometeorites both acting (fitted so the Moon's bright rays fade over about a billion years, Grier et al. 2001)
share of the weathering done by the star's wind at 1 AU; the rest by micrometeorites, taken as the same at any distance (Pieters and Noble 2016)

references: Grier, J. A., McEwen, A. S., Lucey, P. G., Milazzo, M. and Strom, R. G. 2001, Journal of Geophysical Research 106, 32847: the optical maturity of the ejecta of large rayed lunar craters; bright rays fade as their soil matures, over about a billion years. doi:10.1029/1999JE001160

Pieters, C. M. and Noble, S. K. 2016, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets 121, 1865: space weathering on airless bodies; solar wind ions and micrometeorites both make nanophase iron that darkens and reddens soil. doi:10.1002/2016JE005128

equation.name: How long bare ground has lain open to space
equation.formula:
rate = fw * w * clamp(o, 0, 1) + (1 - fw)
M = 1 - exp(-max(t, 0) * rate / tau)

t.name: time the ground has lain open

o.name: wind reaches the ground (1) or is held off by a field (0)

source.text: Grier, J. A. et al. 2001, J. Geophys. Res. 106, 32847
source.where: the fading of lunar crater rays with age

explain.curious: On a world with no air, the star's wind and a rain of dust grains slowly cook the top of the soil, leaving tiny beads of iron that darken it. Fresh craters throw out bright, raw rock; over hundreds of millions of years it weathers dark, so the youngest craters and their rays stand out.
explain.science: Solar wind ions and micrometeorite vapour deposit nanophase iron on soil grains. Maturity is taken to approach 1 exponentially with exposure time; the wind's part scales with its flux (the inverse square of distance) and is held off by a magnetosphere, the micrometeorites' part is taken as the same at any distance. Gardening is folded into the one fitted time.

params.description: mature over fresh reflectance of the same soil at 650 nm
mature over fresh reflectance of the same soil at 550 nm
mature over fresh reflectance of the same soil at 450 nm

references: Hapke, B. 2001, Journal of Geophysical Research 106, 10039: space weathering from Mercury to the asteroid belt; nanophase iron absorbs most strongly at short wavelengths, so mature soil is darker and redder. doi:10.1029/2000JE001338

Lucey, P. G. and Riner, M. A. 2011, Icarus 212, 451: the optical effects of small iron particles that darken but do not redden; reflectance of fresh and mature lunar soils. doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2011.01.009

equation.name: How much darker and redder weathered soil looks
equation.formula:
m = clamp(M, 0, 1)
fr = kr ^ m
fg = kg ^ m
fb = kb ^ m

source.where: nanophase iron and the darkening and reddening of soil

explain.curious: Weathered soil is darker in every colour, but loses most of its blue, so old ground on the Moon looks dark grey-brown while fresh crater ejecta look bright and bluish-grey.
explain.science: Nanophase iron absorbs more strongly at short wavelengths, so the ratio of mature to fresh reflectance falls from red to blue. Each band's ratio at full maturity is a parameter; between fresh and mature the factor is taken as the ratio raised to the maturity, exactly 1 for fresh ground.

references: Showman, A. P. and Malhotra, R. 1999, Science 286, 77: the Galilean satellites; their mean densities fall outward from Io's rock to Callisto's half ice and half rock. doi:10.1126/science.286.5437.77

equation.name: How much of a small world is ice
equation.formula:
w0 = (1 / rho - 1 / rr) / (1 / ri - 1 / rr)
w = if rho <= 0 or rr <= ri then 0 else min(max(w0, 0), 1)

w.name: share of the mass that is ice

source.text: Showman, A. P. and Malhotra, R. 1999, Science 286, 77
source.where: ice and rock shares of the Galilean moons from their densities

explain.curious: A world lighter than rock for its size must be part ice. Europa is only a little lighter than rock, so it has a thin ice shell; Ganymede and Callisto are about half ice.
explain.science: Rock and ice are mixed by volume at their low-pressure densities. Self-compression is left out, which is fair for moons and dwarf planets but makes the bigger icy moons come out somewhat drier than they are (Ganymede about 0.3 against about 0.45 from its moment of inertia).

params.description: rate at which starlight breaks up a water molecule at 1 AU, per second (Huebner et al. 1992, quiet Sun)

references: Fray, N. and Schmitt, B. 2009, Planetary and Space Science 57, 2053: sublimation of ices of astrophysical interest, a bibliographic review; the vapour curves the data sheet's Look up reads. doi:10.1016/j.pss.2009.09.011

Huebner, W. F., Keady, J. J. and Lyon, S. P. 1992, Astrophysics and Space Science 195, 1: solar photo rates for planetary atmospheres and atmospheric pollutants; a water molecule at 1 AU is broken up by sunlight about once a day (rate about 1.2e-5 per second under the quiet Sun). doi:10.1007/BF00644558

Watson, K., Murray, B. C. and Brown, H. 1961, Journal of Geophysical Research 66, 3033: the behaviour of volatiles on the lunar surface; open ice sublimes away on the warm Moon and survives only in cold traps. doi:10.1029/JZ066i009p03033
atoms.shown: L = p √(M/2πRT) (1 − e^(−t_hop k (au/d)²) + (1+λ)e^(−λ)) t / ρ

equation.name: How much open ice an airless world loses
equation.formula:
flux = p * sqrt(M / (2 * pi * R * T))
v2 = 2 * R * T / M
hop = 2 * sqrt(v2) / g
rate = if d > 0 then k * (au / d) * (au / d) else 0
lam = ve * ve / v2
share = min(1 - exp(-hop * rate) + (1 + lam) * exp(-lam), 1)
L = if p <= 0 or T <= 0 or g <= 0 or ri <= 0 then 0 else flux * share * max(t, 0) / ri

p.name: the ice's vapour pressure at the ground's temperature (Look up)

t.name: time the ice has lain open

source.text: Watson, K., Murray, B. C. and Brown, H. 1961, J. Geophys. Res. 66, 3033
source.where: why ice cannot lie open on the warm Moon

explain.curious: Ice left out on an airless world slowly turns straight to vapour. Most of the vapour hops and lands again, but some is broken up by sunlight in flight or flies off into space. Near the Sun the Moon would lose a kilometres-thick ice sheet in a blink of geological time; at Jupiter, where ice is far colder, almost nothing is lost, so its moons keep icy ground.
explain.science: Sublimation flux from the Hertz-Knudsen relation with a sticking coefficient of 1 and the vapour pressure from Fray and Schmitt's fits. Molecules move on ballistic hops of about 2v/g with v the most probable speed; per hop a share 1 − e^(−t_hop J) is photolysed (J the photo rate, falling as 1/d²) and a share (1 + λ)e^(−λ) escapes, λ = v_esc²/v² (Jeans). The rest lands again, so the net loss is the flux times that share. Sputtering and cold-trapping are left out.

params.description: time for open ice ground to come within 1/e of a full dark lag (fitted to Callisto and Ganymede's old ground, Moore et al. 1999)

references: Moore, J. M. et al. 1999, Icarus 140, 294: mass movement and landform degradation on the icy Galilean satellites; sublimation leaves a dark lag of rock and dust over Callisto's ice, which shows bright in fresh craters. doi:10.1006/icar.1999.6132

Spencer, J. R. 1987, Icarus 69, 297: thermal segregation of water ice on the Galilean satellites; sublimed ice leaves a dark lag on the warm ground and frosts the cold. doi:10.1016/0019-1035(87)90107-8
atoms.shown: D = 1 − e^(−t/τ), R = (1 − D) R_ice + D R_dust

equation.name: How old icy ground goes dark
equation.formula:
D = if tau <= 0 then 0 else 1 - exp(-max(t, 0) / tau)
R = (1 - D) * ri + D * rd

t.name: time the ground has lain open

tau.name: time to build a dark lag

D.name: share of the ground under a dark lag

source.where: the dark lag left on icy ground

explain.curious: Icy moons are not all white. Old icy ground slowly gathers a dark skin of dust and rock left behind as the ice turns to vapour and grains rain in from space. Young ground, like Europa's or a fresh crater's, is still clean bright ice; Callisto's ancient ground is dark.
explain.science: The lag's areal share approaches 1 exponentially with exposure age, with one time fitted to Callisto and Ganymede; the ground's reflectance mixes clean ice and dark dust by area. Sublimation's dependence on temperature and the infall rate's on distance are folded into the one fitted time.
